sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Compose hierarchies of agents, delegate via LLM-driven transfer, and choose between sub-agents vs AgentTool

Day 10 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Explain how `sub_agents=[...]` on an LlmAgent auto-generates a delegation tool per child

- Use `transfer_to_agent` (pre-built tool and programmatic `tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent`) to hand off control

- Distinguish **sub-agents** (control fully transfers) from **AgentTool** (control returns to parent)

- Apply `disallow_transfer_to_parent` and `disallow_transfer_to_peers` to constrain the transfer graph

- Design router + specialist and coordinator + worker hierarchies using `description` as the routing signal

sections.title: 1. Why Multi-Agent?
sections.body:
Single-agent systems hit a wall quickly. You start with one friendly assistant, then someone says "let it also book flights" — so you add a tool. Then "let it query our CRM" — another tool. By tool fifteen, the LLM is drowning in JSON schemas, your system prompt is 8 KB, and the model starts calling the wrong tool 20% of the time. Token costs explode, latency triples, and debugging becomes archaeology.

The fix is decomposition: split the workload into focused **sub-agents**, each with a tight instruction and a small tool set, and have a parent agent route work between them. Google ADK makes this idiomatic — you write `LlmAgent(name="router", sub_agents=[weather, capital, math])` and ADK **auto-generates a delegation tool per subagent**, named after the subagent itself. The parent LLM then chooses to "call weather_agent" the same way it would call any other tool.

Two transfer semantics matter. **`transfer_to_agent`** fully hands control to the child — the child owns the conversation until it (or the user) decides to come back. This is the right model for hierarchical chat experiences (a router that says "you want weather? talk to weather_agent") and for specialist workers that need to run their own tool loop. **`AgentTool`** is different: the child runs once, returns an answer, and the parent **summarizes and continues its own turn** — perfect for "summarize this for me" or "translate this paragraph" style delegation where the parent stays in charge.

Today you'll build all four canonical patterns: a router with specialists, a deeper three-level hierarchy, an AgentTool delegation pipeline, and a restricted transfer graph where some handoffs are forbidden. By the end, you'll be able to look at any multi-agent use case and confidently choose sub-agent vs AgentTool vs Remote A2A (which we'll cover in depth on Day 14).

💡 Key Concept

ADK's transfer mechanism is **LLM-driven, not code-driven**. The parent doesn't hard-code `if "weather" in user_msg: route_to(weather_agent)` — instead, ADK exposes each subagent as a *tool* whose description is the subagent's `description` field. The LLM reads these descriptions and decides delegation. This means **the `description` field is the single most important routing signal** — write it like you're writing the tool's docstring for the LLM.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
Five ideas underpin every multi-agent system in ADK. We'll walk through each, then assemble them into working examples.

### 2.1 The `sub_agents=[...]` constructor field

Any `LlmAgent` (and any `BaseAgent` subclass) accepts a `sub_agents=[...]` parameter at construction time. Children can themselves have sub-agents, forming an arbitrarily deep tree. When you register children this way, ADK does **not** add them to the parent's `tools=[...]` list directly; instead, at invocation time, ADK walks the tree and synthesizes a `transfer_to_<child_name>` delegation tool per subagent, then injects those tools into the parent's LLM request.

The result is that the parent LLM "sees" each subagent as a callable tool whose name matches the subagent's `name` and whose description matches the subagent's `description`. The parent has no idea this is happening — from its perspective, `weather_agent` is just another tool. When the LLM decides to call it, ADK intercepts the call and triggers a **full control transfer** to that subagent.

Crucially, transfer is *not* a synchronous RPC. The child takes over the conversation: subsequent events come from the child's author, the child runs its own tool loop, and only when the child completes (or decides to transfer somewhere else) does the user get a final response. This is why `description` matters so much — it's the only signal the parent LLM has to decide whether to delegate.

### 2.2 LLM-driven `transfer_to_agent` (auto-injected + pre-built)

There are **two ways** to invoke a transfer:

**1. Implicit / LLM-driven (the common case).** ADK injects a `transfer_to_<child>` tool per subagent. The parent LLM calls it like any other tool — ADK intercepts and transfers. You write no code for this; it happens automatically when you put agents in `sub_agents=[...]`.

**2. Explicit / programmatic.** Inside any tool, you can force a transfer by writing to the `ToolContext.actions` object:

```python
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

def escalate_to_human(tool_context: ToolContext, issue: str) -> dict:
    """Escalate a tricky customer issue to a human-support sub-agent."""
    tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent = "human_support_agent"
    return {"status": "transferring", "issue": issue}
```

ADK also ships a pre-built tool that does exactly this, intended for use by subagents that want to hand off:

```python
from google.adk.tools import transfer_to_agent
```

The pre-built `transfer_to_agent` is convenient because it works without a custom wrapper, and the LLM knows its signature. Use the programmatic form when you need to set a transfer conditionally inside business logic (e.g., "if confidence < 0.5, transfer to escalation agent").

### 2.3 Sub-agent vs AgentTool vs Remote A2A

ADK offers **three delegation primitives**. They look similar but have very different control-flow semantics — choosing wrong will give you mysterious bugs.

| Pattern | How child runs | Control after child | State sharing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sub-agent** (`sub_agents=[...]`) | Full takeover; child runs its own LLM loop | Child owns conversation; parent dormant until child/user comes back | Child sees `session.state` and `temp:` prefix from parent's invocation context |
| **AgentTool** (`AgentTool(agent=...)`) | Child runs exactly once, returns text | Parent receives text as tool result; parent continues its turn | Child runs in same session; can read/write state, but parent must explicitly read `output_key` if it wants the formatted answer |
| **Remote A2A** (`RemoteA2aAgent`) | Child runs over network via A2A protocol | Network RPC returns; parent summarizes | None automatically — marshalling is up to you |

**Rule of thumb**: if the user would naturally switch conversational partners ("now let me talk to billing"), use **sub-agents**. If the parent should remain the conversational lead and just wants a focused subtask done ("translate this for me, then continue"), use **AgentTool**. If the worker is owned by another team or service, use **Remote A2A**.

### 2.4 Restricting transfers with `disallow_transfer_to_*`

By default, any subagent can transfer to any sibling or back to its parent. That freedom is great during prototyping but dangerous in production — a billing subagent might "helpfully" transfer a confused user to the marketing agent, leaking scope.

ADK exposes two boolean flags on `LlmAgent` to constrain the transfer graph:

- **`disallow_transfer_to_parent=True`** — the subagent cannot hand control back up to its parent. Useful for leaf specialists that should *resolve or fail*, not punt upward.
- **`disallow_transfer_to_peers=True`** — the subagent cannot transfer to its siblings. Useful for "lanes" — e.g., a refund agent that must not be able to send users to the sales agent.

Combined with deliberate tree shape, these flags let you express policies: "support → billing → refund" with refund as a terminal leaf that can only complete or escalate (via `escalate=True` if inside a `LoopAgent`).

These restrictions are enforced at the runtime layer, not the LLM layer — even if the model emits a transfer call to a forbidden target, ADK raises a clear error rather than silently executing it. This makes the policy auditable and testable.

### 2.5 Hierarchy design patterns: router + specialists, coordinator + workers

Two recurring shapes dominate real ADK deployments:

**Router + specialists.** A flat parent whose only job is classification. The router has no tools of its own (or very few); its `instruction` is essentially "decide which specialist should handle this and transfer to it." Each specialist has its own tools, schemas, and instructions. This pattern is best when domains are *disjoint* (weather vs capital vs math) and the user's query maps cleanly to one specialist.

**Coordinator + workers.** A parent that decomposes a complex goal into subtasks, delegates each to a worker, then synthesizes results. Workers might run sequentially (coordinator waits for each) or in parallel (via `ParallelAgent` from Day 11). This pattern is best when the user's goal is *composite* — e.g., "plan my trip" needs weather + flights + hotels + itinerary.

The decisive question: **does the user need to talk to a specialist, or do they need the parent to coordinate?** If talk-to-specialist, use a router. If parent-coordinates, use a coordinator with `AgentTool` (so the parent stays in charge) or `Workflow` (Day 12) for deterministic orchestration.

sections.title: 3. Multi-Agent Hierarchy — ASCII Architecture
sections.body:
This diagram shows the canonical router + specialists tree with the auto-injected delegation tools ADK synthesizes at runtime.

```
MULTI-AGENT HIERARCHY (router + specialists)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                        ┌──────────────────┐
                        │   router_agent   │   (root_agent)
                        │  model: gemini   │
                        │  tools: []       │   ← no own tools!
                        │  sub_agents:[…]  │
                        └────────┬─────────┘
                                 │  ADK auto-injects delegation tools:
                                 │   • weather_agent()
                                 │   • capital_agent()
                                 │   • math_agent()
          ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
          │                      │                      │
          ▼                      ▼                      ▼
  ┌───────────────┐      ┌───────────────┐      ┌───────────────┐
  │ weather_agent │      │ capital_agent │      │  math_agent   │
  │  tools:       │      │  tools:       │      │  tools:       │
  │   get_weather │      │   get_capital │      │   add, sub,   │
  │  output_key:  │      │  output_key:  │      │   mul, div    │
  │   weather_out │      │   capital_out │      │  output_key:  │
  └───────┬───────┘      └───────────────┘      │   math_out    │
          │                                      └───────────────┘
          │ transfer_to_agent="math_agent"
          │   ← programmatic transfer (allowed by default)
          │
          ▼
    control lands in math_agent's LLM loop

RESTRICTIONS:
  disallow_transfer_to_parent=True  → child can't punt back to router
  disallow_transfer_to_peers=True   → child can't hop to sibling
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

sections.title: 4. Mermaid — Travel Planner Delegation Flow
sections.body:
The same pattern as a travel planner: a root agent delegates to weather, flight, and hotel specialists. Each specialist owns its own tools. Control transfers via the auto-injected delegation tools.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
ROOT[Root Agent
travel_planner]
ROOT -->|transfer_to_agent| W[weather_agent
mode: single_turn]
ROOT -->|transfer_to_agent| F[flight_agent
mode: task]
ROOT -->|transfer_to_agent| H[hotel_agent
mode: chat]
W --> W1[get_weather tool]
F --> F1[search_flights tool]
F --> F2[book_flight tool]
H --> H1[search_hotels tool]
style ROOT fill:#1A73E8,color:#fff
style W fill:#34A853,color:#fff
style F fill:#FBBC04,color:#202124
style H fill:#EA4335,color:#fff
```

🚀 Pro Tip

When designing your hierarchy, draw this Mermaid diagram first. If you find yourself writing "router routes to router", you've over-engineered — flatten the tree. A good rule: no agent should have more than 5–7 direct children, because the parent LLM has to read all their descriptions on every turn.

sections.title: 5. Visual Comparison — Sub-agent vs AgentTool vs Remote A2A
sections.body:
The PNG below (generated by `adk_visuals.day10_multi_agent_patterns`) compares the three delegation primitives side by side. The decisive question is **what happens to control after the child runs**.

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename="images/day10_multi_agent_patterns.png"))
```

| | Sub-agent | AgentTool | Remote A2A |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control after child | Child keeps talking | Returns to parent | Returns to parent |
| Child runs | Own LLM loop | Once | Once (over network) |
| Setup | `sub_agents=[...]` | `tools=[AgentTool(agent=...)]` | `sub_agents=[RemoteA2aAgent(...)]` |
| Best for | Hierarchical chat | Focused subtask | Cross-service worker |

sections.title: 6. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
1. **Example 1** — Two-agent router: weather + capital under a root router
2. **Example 2** — Three-agent hierarchy: router + math + science + history specialists
3. **Example 3** — AgentTool delegation: parent delegates summarization, continues its turn
4. **Example 4** — Restricted transfers: `disallow_transfer_to_parent` + `disallow_transfer_to_peers`

Example 1: Two-Agent Router: Weather + Capital

The minimal multi-agent system — a router with two specialists and zero routing code

This is the "Hello World" of multi-agent ADK. Note three things:

1. The **root router** has an empty `tools=[]` list — it owns no functionality of its own.
2. Each **specialist** is a normal `LlmAgent` with its own tools, instruction, and `output_key`.
3. The `sub_agents=[weather_agent, capital_agent]` line on the router is the *only* multi-agent plumbing.

At runtime, ADK inspects the router's `sub_agents`, sees two children, and synthesizes two tools — `weather_agent` and `capital_agent` — whose descriptions are the children's `description` strings. The router LLM picks the right one based on the user's query. You wrote zero `if/else` routing code.

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: Two-Agent Router
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent

# ── Specialist: weather ────────────────────────────────────────
def get_weather(city: str) -> dict:
    """Returns the current weather for a city.

    Args:
        city (str): Name of the city.
    """
    mock = {"Tokyo": "22°C, partly cloudy", "Paris": "15°C, rain", "Cairo": "32°C, sunny"}
    return {"city": city, "weather": mock.get(city, "20°C, clear")}

weather_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="weather_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions about the weather in any city. Delegate here whenever the user asks about weather, temperature, rain, or forecasts.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a weather specialist. Use get_weather to fetch conditions. "
        "Reply in one short sentence with the city, temperature, and condition."
    ),
    tools=[get_weather],
    output_key="weather_result",
)

# ── Specialist: capital cities ─────────────────────────────────
def get_capital(country: str) -> dict:
    """Returns the capital city of a country.

    Args:
        country (str): Name of the country.
    """
    caps = {"Japan": "Tokyo", "France": "Paris", "Egypt": "Cairo", "Brazil": "Brasília"}
    return {"country": country, "capital": caps.get(country, "Unknown")}

capital_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="capital_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions about capital cities of countries. Delegate here whenever the user asks 'what is the capital of X' or similar.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a geography specialist. Use get_capital to look up the capital. "
        "Reply in one short sentence."
    ),
    tools=[get_capital],
    output_key="capital_result",
)

# ── Router (root_agent) ────────────────────────────────────────
root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="router_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Routes user questions to the right specialist.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a router. Based on the user's question, delegate to the matching "
        "specialist by calling its tool. Do not answer yourself. The specialists are:\n"
        "- weather_agent: weather, temperature, forecasts\n"
        "- capital_agent: capital cities of countries"
    ),
    # No tools=[] — ADK auto-injects weather_agent() and capital_agent() tools
    sub_agents=[weather_agent, capital_agent],
)

# Inspect what ADK will inject
print(f"Root: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Children: {[c.name for c in root_agent.sub_agents]}")
print(f"Child descriptions ADK will use as tool descriptions:")
for c in root_agent.sub_agents:
    print(f"  - {c.name}: {c.description[:60]}…")
```

**Output**

```text
Root: router_agent\nChildren: ['weather_agent', 'capital_agent']\nChild descriptions ADK will use as tool descriptions:\n  - weather_agent: Answers questions about the weather in any city. Delegate…\n  - capital_agent: Answers questions about capital cities of countries. Delega…\n
```

```python
# Run via ADK CLI
adk run my_router_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with router_agent.\n\n>>> What's the weather in Tokyo?\n[router_agent] delegating to weather_agent…\n[weather_agent] calling tool get_weather(city='Tokyo')\n[weather_agent] tool result: {'city': 'Tokyo', 'weather': '22°C, partly cloudy'}\n\nIt's 22°C and partly cloudy in Tokyo right now.\n\n>>> What is the capital of France?\n[router_agent] delegating to capital_agent…\n[capital_agent] calling tool get_capital(country='France')\n[capital_agent] tool result: {'country': 'France', 'capital': 'Paris'}\n\nThe capital of France is Paris.\n
```

💡 Key Concept

Notice the `author` field on each event changes as control transfers. Events from the router are authored by `router_agent`; once transferred, subsequent events are authored by `weather_agent`. This is how you audit multi-agent runs — the event stream tells you exactly which agent owned each turn.

Example 2: Three-Agent Hierarchy: Math + Science + History

A deeper router with three specialists and explicit output_key state-passing

Now we scale to three specialists and add two production patterns:

1. **Each specialist writes to its own `output_key`** so downstream agents (or the router itself on a future turn) can read prior answers from `session.state`.
2. **The router's instruction names each specialist's `output_key`** so it can decide when a follow-up question should consult prior state vs re-delegate.

We also add a `generate_content_config` with low temperature on the router — routing decisions should be deterministic, not creative.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: Three-Specialist Router
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.genai import types

# ── Math specialist ────────────────────────────────────────────
def add(a: float, b: float) -> dict:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return {"a": a, "b": b, "sum": a + b}

def multiply(a: float, b: float) -> dict:
    """Multiply two numbers."""
    return {"a": a, "b": b, "product": a * b}

math_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="math_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Solves arithmetic problems. Delegate here for any question involving addition, multiplication, subtraction, or division of numbers.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a math specialist. Use add() or multiply() to compute. "
        "Always show the calculation, then the result. Be concise."
    ),
    tools=[add, multiply],
    output_key="math_result",
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(temperature=0.0),
)

# ── Science specialist ─────────────────────────────────────────
def lookup_science_fact(topic: str) -> dict:
    """Look up a science fact about a topic (e.g. 'photosynthesis')."""
    facts = {
        "photosynthesis": "Plants convert sunlight, CO2, and water into glucose and oxygen.",
        "gravity": "Gravity accelerates falling objects at ~9.8 m/s² near Earth's surface.",
        "dna": "DNA stores genetic information as a sequence of four bases: A, T, C, G.",
    }
    return {"topic": topic, "fact": facts.get(topic.lower(), "No fact available.")}

science_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="science_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Explains science concepts. Delegate here for any question about physics, biology, chemistry, or natural phenomena.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a science specialist. Use lookup_science_fact(topic=...) "
        "to retrieve a fact, then explain it in 1–2 sentences for a layperson."
    ),
    tools=[lookup_science_fact],
    output_key="science_result",
)

# ── History specialist ─────────────────────────────────────────
def lookup_historical_event(year: int) -> dict:
    """Look up a notable historical event for a given year."""
    events = {
        1969: "Apollo 11 lands on the Moon; Neil Armstrong takes first step.",
        1989: "Fall of the Berlin Wall; beginning of the end of the Cold War.",
        1492: "Christopher Columbus reaches the Americas.",
    }
    return {"year": year, "event": events.get(year, "No recorded event for that year.")}

history_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="history_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions about historical events. Delegate here for any question about history, dates, wars, or famous figures.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a history specialist. Use lookup_historical_event(year=...) "
        "to find an event, then describe it in 1–2 sentences."
    ),
    tools=[lookup_historical_event],
    output_key="history_result",
)

# ── Router ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="root_router",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="A multi-subject tutor that routes questions to the right specialist.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a tutor router. Read the user's question and delegate to the matching "
        "specialist by calling its tool. Do not answer yourself.\n\n"
        "Specialists:\n"
        "- math_agent: arithmetic, calculations, numbers\n"
        "- science_agent: physics, biology, chemistry, natural phenomena\n"
        "- history_agent: dates, events, historical figures\n\n"
        "If the user asks a follow-up that references a previous answer, you may "
        "read state: math_result, science_result, history_result."
    ),
    sub_agents=[math_agent, science_agent, history_agent],
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(temperature=0.1),
)

print(f"Router '{root_agent.name}' with {len(root_agent.sub_agents)} specialists:")
for s in root_agent.sub_agents:
    print(f"  • {s.name}  (output_key={s.output_key})  tools={len(s.tools)}")
```

**Output**

```text
Router 'root_router' with 3 specialists:\n  • math_agent  (output_key=math_result)  tools=2\n  • science_agent  (output_key=science_result)  tools=1\n  • history_agent  (output_key=history_result)  tools=1\n
```

```python
# Sample session — note how the router hands off to the right specialist each time
adk run my_tutor_agent
```

**Output**

```text
>>> What is 25 times 4?\n[root_router] delegating to math_agent…\n[math_agent] calling multiply(a=25, b=4) → {a:25, b:4, product:100}\n25 × 4 = 100.\n\n>>> Explain photosynthesis.\n[root_router] delegating to science_agent…\n[science_agent] calling lookup_science_fact(topic='photosynthesis')\nPhotosynthesis is how plants convert sunlight, CO2, and water into glucose and oxygen.\n\n>>> What happened in 1969?\n[root_router] delegating to history_agent…\n[history_agent] calling lookup_historical_event(year=1969)\nIn 1969, Apollo 11 landed on the Moon and Neil Armstrong took the first step.\n
```

🚀 Pro Tip

The router never sees the specialist's tool results directly — those belong to the specialist. But the specialist's final text answer is saved to `session.state[output_key]`, which means a *future* router turn *can* read it. This is the canonical way to give a router "memory of what specialists answered" without coupling them.

Example 3: AgentTool Delegation: Parent Stays in Charge

Use AgentTool so the parent delegates a focused subtask, then continues its own turn

Now contrast Example 1's *transfer* pattern with *AgentTool* delegation. Here the parent agent has its own job (translate a paragraph) and wants the summarizer to do a focused subtask (summarize it first), then the parent continues with translation.

The key constructor change: instead of `sub_agents=[summarizer]`, we use `tools=[AgentTool(agent=summarizer, skip_summarization=True)]`. The `skip_summarization=True` flag tells ADK **not** to run the parent LLM again on the summarizer's output — return the raw text as the tool result. Without it, the parent would re-summarize the summary, which is wasteful.

The control-flow consequence: when the parent calls `summarizer`, the summarizer runs **once** and returns text. The parent then decides what to do next (here: translate the summary). The user never "talks to" the summarizer — it's a private subroutine.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: AgentTool Delegation
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.agent_tool import AgentTool

# ── Summarizer sub-agent (used as a TOOL, not as a sub-agent) ──
summarizer = LlmAgent(
    name="summarizer",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Summarizes long text into 2-3 bullet points.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a summarizer. Given text, produce 2-3 concise bullet points "
        "capturing the key ideas. Output only the bullets, no preamble."
    ),
    # No tools — this is a pure-LLM sub-agent
)

# ── Parent: translator that summarizes first, then translates ──
root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="translate_and_summarize",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Summarizes long English text and translates the summary to Spanish.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a translation assistant. When the user gives you a long English text:\n"
        "1. First call the 'summarizer' tool to extract the key points.\n"
        "2. Then translate those bullet points into Spanish.\n"
        "3. Reply with both the English summary and the Spanish translation, clearly labeled."
    ),
    tools=[
        # AgentTool wraps the summarizer as a callable tool.
        # skip_summarization=True → return the summarizer's raw output,
        # do NOT run the parent LLM again to "summarize the summary".
        AgentTool(agent=summarizer, skip_summarization=True),
    ],
    # NOTE: NO sub_agents=[summarizer] here — that would trigger a full
    # transfer instead of a one-shot tool call. The two are mutually exclusive
    # for a given child agent.
)

print(f"Parent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Tools: {[t.name if hasattr(t,'name') else t.__class__.__name__ for t in root_agent.tools]}")
print(f"Sub-agents: {getattr(root_agent, 'sub_agents', [])}")
```

**Output**

```text
Parent: translate_and_summarize\nTools: ['summarizer']\nSub-agents: []\n
```

```bash
adk run my_translator
```

**Output**

```text
>>> The Apollo program was a series of space missions flown by NASA between 1961 and 1972.\n    It culminated in the first human landing on the Moon in 1969. The program cost about\n    $25 billion (>$150 billion in 2024 dollars) and employed 400,000 people at its peak.\n\n[translate_and_summarize] calling summarizer(text=…)\n[summarizer] returned 3 bullets\n\n── English summary ──────────────\n• NASA's Apollo program ran 1961–1972.\n• First Moon landing was in 1969.\n• Cost ~$25B (>$150B today); 400k staff at peak.\n\n── Spanish translation ──────────\n• El programa Apolo de la NASA funcionó de 1961 a 1972.\n• El primer alunizaje fue en 1969.\n• Costó ~$25 mil millones (>$150 mil millones hoy); 400 mil empleados en su apogeo.\n
```

⚠️ Important

**Do not register the same child as both `sub_agents=[child]` AND `tools=[AgentTool(agent=child)]`.** The two mechanisms have incompatible control-flow semantics — a sub-agent expects to take over the conversation, while an AgentTool expects to be called and return. Pick one per child. If you need both behaviors, instantiate the agent twice with different names (e.g., `summarizer_sub` and `summarizer_tool`).

Example 4: Restricted Transfers: Blocking Parent & Peer Handoffs

Use disallow_transfer_to_parent / disallow_transfer_to_peers to enforce a strict hierarchy

Our final example enforces policy. Consider a customer-support tree:

```
root_support (router)
  ├── billing_agent        (can transfer to: refund_agent)
  │   └── refund_agent     (LEAF — cannot transfer anywhere)
  └── sales_agent          (cannot transfer to billing!)
```

- `billing_agent` may send customers to `refund_agent` (a child), but **not** to `sales_agent` (a peer).
- `refund_agent` is a terminal specialist — it must resolve or fail, **not** punt back up to `billing_agent`.

We achieve this with `disallow_transfer_to_peers=True` on `billing_agent` and `sales_agent`, and `disallow_transfer_to_parent=True` on `refund_agent`. The result is an auditable transfer graph — your security review can show exactly which handoffs are possible.

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: Restricted Transfer Graph
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent

# ── Leaf: refund specialist — cannot punt back up ──────────────
def issue_refund(account_id: str, amount_usd: float) -> dict:
    """Issue a refund to a customer's account."""
    return {"account": account_id, "refunded_usd": amount_usd, "status": "issued"}

refund_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="refund_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Issues refunds. Cannot transfer back to billing or to sales — must resolve here.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a refund specialist. Use issue_refund(account_id, amount_usd). "
        "Always confirm the amount before issuing. You cannot transfer this conversation anywhere else."
    ),
    tools=[issue_refund],
    output_key="refund_result",
    # Enforce leaf status: no transfers anywhere.
    disallow_transfer_to_parent=True,
    disallow_transfer_to_peers=True,
)

# ── billing_agent — can transfer DOWN to refund_agent, not to sales_agent ─
def lookup_invoice(account_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up a customer's last invoice."""
    return {"account": account_id, "last_invoice_usd": 49.99, "due_date": "2026-09-01"}

billing_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="billing_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Handles billing questions and refunds. Delegate here for invoices, charges, or refund requests.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a billing specialist. Use lookup_invoice(account_id). "
        "If the user wants a refund, transfer to refund_agent. "
        "You cannot transfer to sales_agent — billing and sales are separate lanes."
    ),
    tools=[lookup_invoice],
    output_key="billing_result",
    sub_agents=[refund_agent],     # refund is a child → can transfer down
    disallow_transfer_to_peers=True,  # cannot hop to sales_agent
)

# ── sales_agent — cannot transfer to billing ──────────────────
def search_products(query: str) -> dict:
    """Search the product catalog."""
    return {"query": query, "matches": ["Pro Plan ($29/mo)", "Team Plan ($99/mo)"]}

sales_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="sales_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Handles product questions and sales. Delegate here for pricing, plans, and product info.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a sales specialist. Use search_products(query). "
        "You cannot transfer to billing_agent — sales and billing are separate lanes."
    ),
    tools=[search_products],
    output_key="sales_result",
    disallow_transfer_to_peers=True,  # cannot hop to billing_agent
)

# ── Root support router ────────────────────────────────────────
root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="support_router",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Customer support router — delegates to billing or sales.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a customer support router. Delegate to billing_agent for invoices, "
        "charges, or refunds. Delegate to sales_agent for products and pricing. "
        "Do not answer yourself."
    ),
    sub_agents=[billing_agent, sales_agent],
)

# Print the enforced policy
print("Transfer policy:")
print(f"  billing_agent → disallow_transfer_to_peers = {billing_agent.disallow_transfer_to_peers}")
print(f"  sales_agent   → disallow_transfer_to_peers = {sales_agent.disallow_transfer_to_peers}")
print(f"  refund_agent  → disallow_transfer_to_parent = {refund_agent.disallow_transfer_to_parent}")
print(f"  refund_agent  → disallow_transfer_to_peers  = {refund_agent.disallow_transfer_to_peers}")
```

**Output**

```text
Transfer policy:\n  billing_agent → disallow_transfer_to_peers = True\n  sales_agent   → disallow_transfer_to_peers = True\n  refund_agent  → disallow_transfer_to_parent = True\n  refund_agent  → disallow_transfer_to_peers  = True\n
```

```python
# Demonstrate allowed vs forbidden transfers
adk run my_support_agent
```

**Output**

```text
>>> I was charged twice, I want a refund!\n[support_router] delegating to billing_agent…\n[billing_agent] looking up invoice for account acct_001 → $49.99 due 2026-09-01\n[billing_agent] refund requested — transferring to refund_agent (child)\n[refund_agent] confirming refund of $49.99 to acct_001\n[refund_agent] calling issue_refund(account_id='acct_001', amount_usd=49.99)\nRefund of $49.99 issued to account acct_001. Confirmation #RF-20260813-001.\n\n>>> Now can you tell me about Pro Plan pricing?\n[refund_agent] attempted transfer to sales_agent → BLOCKED by disallow_transfer_to_peers\n[refund_agent] attempted transfer to billing_agent → BLOCKED by disallow_transfer_to_parent\nERROR: refund_agent is a terminal specialist. Please start a new conversation.\n
```

🚀 Pro Tip

**Test your transfer policy with negative cases.** A common mistake is to only test the "happy path" (billing → refund succeeds) and forget the "sad path" (refund → sales should fail). Write a conformance test (`adk conformance`) that asserts each forbidden transfer raises the expected error. This turns your security review from "trust me" into "here's the test report".

sections.title: Day 10 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **`sub_agents=[...]` on an LlmAgent auto-generates a delegation tool per child — the parent LLM sees each child as a callable tool**

- **`transfer_to_agent` fully hands control to the child agent — child owns the conversation; parent dormant until child/user returns**

- **Two ways to invoke transfer: implicit (LLM calls auto-injected tool) or explicit (`tool_context.actions.transfer_to_agent = 'name'`)**

- **Sub-agent** = control transfers · **AgentTool** = control returns · **Remote A2A** = network RPC (Day 14)

- **The `description` field on each subagent is the parent LLM's ONLY routing signal — write it like a tool docstring**

- **`disallow_transfer_to_parent=True` blocks upward handoffs; `disallow_transfer_to_peers=True` blocks sibling handoffs**

- **Never register the same child as both `sub_agents=[child]` and `tools=[AgentTool(agent=child)]` — semantics conflict**
